title: Release candidate 2 on paper, batch 1: the first three pages
how: Dinis printed the candidate's PDF (168 A4 pages, spiral bound) and marked it with a pen; photographs of the marked pages were sent to the journalist, who read the handwriting, confirmed the one uncertain note with Dinis, and drew each page three ways: the photograph with numbered callouts, a clean redraw with the marks in place for anyone to read, and a sketch of the page after the change.

parts.title: Before you start
parts.intro: Five chapters before the argument starts. Who this book is for and what it is for, why I think you are lucky to be here, one chapter on graphs because everything after it is one, how to find out which kind of developer you are, and why the path only makes sense afterwards. Read these first; then go where your map says.

parts.title: The frame
parts.intro: The frame the rest of the book hangs on. What generative AI is and is not, what happens between your prompt and the answer, why the word developer now means anyone who can brief an agent, and the founder's way of building: explore first, call it what it is, then hand it over.

parts.title: Getting the job, or making it
parts.intro: The part the first edition called your CV, rewritten for 2026, for the reader going into a job. You are hired for a workflow now, not a language; the way to show it is to act as the job you want before anyone gives it to you; and the place to show it is a newsroom of your own. In 2018 I said act like a founder. Now you can be one, and the next parts say how.

parts.title: Working with agents
parts.intro: How to work with the colleague that takes everything literally, whether it works for your employer or for your company. Where the agent runs and what it can reach, the brief as the unit of work, the mistakes that become rules, and why one focused session per job beats one long chat.

parts.title: Direction and judgement
parts.intro: The scarce skill. When the making is cheap, direction and judgement are what you are paid for, and what a founder lives or dies by: which doors can be reopened, who answers for a decision an agent made, and the chapter the first edition promised and never wrote, on facts, evidence and the record.

parts.title: Start the company
parts.intro: The centre of this edition. Execution just got cheap, so the person who knows the problem can build the first answer; then ship it and see if they miss it, price it and give it away, sell, decide whether to raise at all, and make the company itself real: the UK, Portugal, Lithuania, the European Union. From experience, mine and the people I work with; not legal or tax advice.

parts.title: Build it without a server
parts.intro: Build it so that there is nothing to run at three in the morning. Serverless, for real; privacy by design, with data encrypted on the user's device on a server that cannot read it; control of the agents your company runs on; open source and who pays for it; and the only definition of shipped that counts: the user has it.

parts.title: The long game
parts.intro: What lasts. Graphs as memory for the person you will be, and the civic responsibility that comes with knowing how the machines work, for a small country and for a continent.

parts.title: Hands on, 2026
parts.intro: The practical part, dated 2026 and renewed every year, inside the book. Eleven workflows you can follow this afternoon, from an agentic workflow from zero to forming your company, the credits and programmes as they stand this year, your first price and your first ten customers, and a serverless product shipped in a weekend.

parts.title: How this book was made, and what you made
parts.intro: The last part is the process, because the process is as much the product as the book: a repository for the official versions, a vault for the working ones, roles with folders, articles as briefs, decisions as files, a graph that says where every idea came from, release candidates and a review board. And the measure: the companies you create from it, and how to tell us.
